Contribute

You can contribute to PyAEDT-MCP in several ways:

Answer questions on the PyAEDT-MCP Discussions page.

Report bugs or request features on the PyAEDT-MCP Issues page.

Submit pull requests with bug fixes, new features, or documentation improvements.

title: Contribute > Answer discussions
text:
Answer discussions

Answering questions on the PyAEDT-MCP Discussions page
is the easiest way to contribute. Only a GitHub account is required. Engaging with discussions
deepens your understanding of the project and helps other users who are facing similar issues.
This makes the repository more welcoming and inclusive.

title: Contribute > Post issues

Use the PyAEDT-MCP Issues page to
report bugs, suggest improvements, or request features.

When possible, use these issue templates:

📖 Documentation issue: Suggest modifications needed to the documentation.

🎓 Adding an example: Propose a new example for the library.

💡 New feature: Propose a new capability.

If your issue does not fit into any existing category, click

title: The toolsets.py module > Description
text:
Description

Toolset definitions for PyAnsys MCP service discovery.

Exposes the toolsets://definition MCP resource that groups every tool
registered on PyAEDT-MCP into logical, user-facing categories.
Each toolset entry follows the schema agreed across the Ansys MCP family:

{"name": str, "description": str, "skill": str, "tools": list[str]}

The catalogue is a pure discovery aid — it does not affect tool visibility,
gating, or runtime behavior. Visibility is still controlled by the existing
REQUIRES_AEDT_TAG / aedt_tools / locked_connection tags applied
in ansys.aedt.mcp.tools.

title: The lanes package > Description
text:
Description

Opt-in lanes mode: share or isolate AEDT sessions across MCP clients.

Enabled with ansys-aedt-mcp --lanes. Without that flag none of these
modules is imported and the server behaves exactly as before.

A lane is a long-lived ansys-aedt-mcp HTTP backend that owns at most one
AEDT session. A stdio routing proxy exposes the regular tools plus lane
management tools and forwards each call to the selected lane.

title: The dashboard.py module > Description
text:
Description

Local, read-only status dashboard for lanes.

Serves one HTML page and one JSON endpoint on 127.0.0.1. Status comes
only from cheap, static sources: the registry file, process liveness, TCP
connects to the registered ports, and the tail of each lane log. The
dashboard never opens an MCP session, so it cannot load or be blocked by a
busy lane.

title: The proxy.py module > Description
text:
Description

Stdio routing proxy that multiplexes AEDT sessions (“lanes”).

The proxy is what an MCP client starts with ansys-aedt-mcp --lanes. It:

Lists the regular PyAEDT-MCP tools in-process, applying the same tag
filters as the regular CLI. No backend is spawned at startup.

Registers one routing wrapper per tool. Each wrapper forwards the call to
the lane selected in this proxy process, or fails fast when none is.

Adds lane management tools (spawn_lane, switch_lane, and so on)
plus health and recovery helpers.

The selected lane is per proxy process, so every client window gets an
independent view of the same machine-wide fleet.

Run an HFSS patch antenna workflow

This example shows how to run a complete HFSS microstrip patch antenna workflow with
PyAEDT-MCP tools. All steps were validated live against Ansys AEDT

Launch AEDT with non_graphical=False so the GUI is visible and you can

title: Run an HFSS patch antenna workflow > Tool visibility model
text:
Tool visibility model

PyAEDT-MCP uses a connection-aware visibility model. The MCP client sees a small,
focused tool surface first, and additional tools unlock after an AEDT session
exists. This avoids “tool not available - connect first” round-trips and
reduces token cost.

title: Desktop app
text:
Desktop app

The PyAEDT MCP desktop app provides a Windows interface for installing and
updating the managed MCP environment, running the local HTTP server, and
configuring supported coding-agent profiles.

title: Desktop app > First launch
text:
First launch

When the managed environment has not been installed, the app opens a setup
guide. The managed environment is the virtual environment that the PyAEDT
MCP desktop app creates for installing and running PyAEDT MCP.
By default, this environment is available in %APPDATA%\\.pyaedt_mcp.

On the Server tab, choose an install source and MCP version, then
select Install MCP. After installation, the app enables Start Server.
Offline installation prompts for a wheelhouse ZIP for each install or update, without
querying package indexes. The app verifies that the ZIP targets its bundled Python 3.13
runtime before installation. Turn this mode on or off in the Installation section
of the Settings tab; the choice is retained in %APPDATA%\\.pyaedt_mcp\\settings.yaml.
Git branch installation requires online mode.

To reuse an existing local Python environment instead of creating one, select
Use local environment in the first-launch guide. Choose the environment’s
root folder (containing Scripts\python.exe for a virtual environment, or
python.exe for a Conda environment), not its Scripts folder. If PyAEDT
MCP is already installed there, the app enables Start Server immediately.
Otherwise, Install MCP installs it into that environment without creating
a new one.

In Settings, turn on Custom environment to select a folder, or use the
folder selector to change it. Turning the toggle off restores the default
%APPDATA%\.pyaedt_mcp\.venv environment without deleting or modifying the
custom environment. The selection is retained across launches. Stop the server
and wait for any installation or update to finish before switching environments.
Install and update actions modify the selected environment. After switching,
reinstall any Stdio coding-agent profiles so they use the newly selected
environment.

Use the Update MCP button to update an existing managed environment. Choose
Git branch as the install source when testing a repository branch instead
of a published release.

title: Desktop app > Building the Windows executable
text:
Building the Windows executable

From a development checkout, install the desktop dependency group and run
.\scripts\build_windows_installer.ps1 -ExecutableOnly. This command checks
that the desktop GUI imports and its tray image loads before packaging.

title: Desktop app > Server tab
text:
Server tab

Use the Server tab to install or update PyAEDT MCP and to start its local
HTTP transport. The Server log window displays standard output and errors
from the MCP server that the desktop app launches. Use it to confirm startup,
inspect debug output, and diagnose a server that exits unexpectedly.

title: Desktop app > Lanes
text:
Lanes

When lanes are registered on the machine, the Server tab shows a Lanes
section below the server log. Lanes are shared PyAEDT MCP backends started by
coding agents whose profiles use ansys-aedt-mcp --lanes. For more
information, see Lanes. The section is hidden while no lanes
are registered and is refreshed automatically when agents start or stop lanes.

Each lane shows its name, HTTP port, AEDT gRPC port, and uptime. A green
indicator means that the lane process is running and serving its port. A red
indicator means that the lane is not responding. The section provides these
actions:

Stop next to a lane stops that lane and removes it from the registry.
Coding agents routed to the lane lose their backend.

Remove dead lanes drops registry entries whose backend is no longer
running.

Stop all lanes stops every lane process and clears the registry.

The browser button opens the read-only lanes dashboard.

The desktop app manages lanes through the ansys-aedt-mcp --lanes commands of
the selected environment. The dashboard server stops when you exit the app.

title: Desktop app > System tray
text:
System tray

Closing the app window keeps PyAEDT MCP running in the Windows
system tray. To exit the desktop app completely, right-click the PyAEDT MCP
tray icon and select Exit.

The tray menu provides the following actions:

Open window restores the control panel after it has been hidden.

Start Server starts the local HTTP server with the current settings on
the Advanced tab.

Stop Server stops the HTTP server that was started by the desktop app.

Exit stops the local HTTP server, removes the tray icon, and closes the
desktop app.

Settings are retained while the window is hidden. Closing the window does not
stop a running server; use Stop Server or Exit from the tray menu when
the server is no longer needed.

title: Desktop app > Advanced tab
text:
Advanced tab

The desktop app starts the server with --transport http and
--http-host 127.0.0.1. Use AEDT connection and MCP options to
configure the remaining server arguments:

HTTP port sets --http-port. The default is 8080.

AEDT host and gRPC port provide the values for --machine and

--port when Connect on start is selected.

Connect on start adds --connect. The server then connects to the

configured AEDT session at startup and locks that connection for its
lifetime.

Graphical AEDT adds --graphical. Leave it unselected to use the

default non-graphical AEDT mode.

Guidance tools adds --include-context to register the optional AEDT

and PyAEDT workflow guidance tools.

Dynamic tools adds --dynamic-tool-discovery to hide AEDT-only tools

until the server has an AEDT connection.

Debug logging sets FASTMCP_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG for the server process.

For the full list of command-line server options, including --version and
the HTTP CORS settings that are not exposed by the desktop app, see
Advanced configuration.

title: Desktop app > Coding agents tab
text:
Coding agents tab

Select the coding-agent profiles to configure, choose Stdio or HTTP as
the profile transport, and confirm the configuration path for each agent.
Select Install profiles to write the selected configuration files. Use
HTTP only after starting the local HTTP server.

Select Use lanes to write Stdio profiles that start the lanes routing proxy
(ansys-aedt-mcp --lanes), so several agents can share or isolate AEDT
sessions. The MCP options from the Advanced tab are forwarded to every
lane. Lanes require the Stdio transport and do not support Dynamic tools.

title: Overview
text:
Overview

PyAEDT-MCP is a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that lets you use an AI
client with AEDT. It acts as a bridge between your AI client and AEDT.

title: Overview > Main modules
text:
Main modules





Module

Responsibility

server.py

Defines the app, CLI, startup logic, cleanup, transport selection, and typed app context.

tools.py

Implements the AEDT-facing tool surface: connection, project management, scripting, analysis, inspection, and export.

helpers.py

Holds small helpers for endpoint probing, version parsing, and extracting structured AEDT model information.

prompts.py

Builds the system prompt exposed to MCP clients, including the connection workflow and tool-usage rules. It provides useful context for the AI client to understand the server’s capabilities and limitations.

toolsets.py

Publishes the toolsets://definition discovery resource that groups tools into logical categories.

contexts.py

Registers optional guideline tools that are enabled only when the server starts with --include-context.

aedt_helper/startup_code.py

Provides the startup imports and shared helpers loaded into the persistent Python session.

title: Overview > Tool groups
text:
Tool groups

You get a small public tool surface grouped by workflow:

Lifecycle: Check installation, verify connection status, launch and connect to AEDT,
disconnect when needed, and clean up.

Project management: List projects and designs, open projects, save work, and create designs.

Simulation: Analyze the active design and export setup configuration.

Inspection and results: Inspect the model, capture screenshots, read logs, and export
solver results.

Scripting: Run short inline PyAEDT code or a Python file against the current AEDT session.

When --dynamic-tool-discovery is enabled, tools tagged with
REQUIRES_AEDT_TAG are hidden until the server has an active AEDT
connection. This helps save LLM context budget because AEDT-dependent tools
are not advertised by default before a connection exists. Without this flag,
the full tool surface stays visible from startup.

title: Overview > Simple AEDT use cases
text:
Simple AEDT use cases

Here are a few simple workflows you can run through the MCP server:

Check your environment and connect: Verify installation, launch AEDT if
needed, and connect to a running session.

Open and inspect a project: List available projects and designs, open the
one you need, and inspect model information, such as geometry, materials, and boundary conditions.

Run a basic analysis: Analyze the active design and export setup
configuration for review.

Collect quick outputs: Capture a screenshot and export solver results to
share with teammates.

Automate repetitive steps: Use MCP tools and PyAEDT scripts to automate
repeated tasks, iterate faster, and reduce manual errors.

title: The aedt_compat.py module > Description
text:
Description

In-process PyAEDT version fixes applied by lane backends.

PyAEDT treats the newest installed AEDT that is not newer than its
CURRENT_STABLE_AEDT_VERSION as the default. With a newer AEDT installed,
launch_aedt without a version starts the older release, and
connect_to_aedt(port=...) can decide the port belongs to another AEDT
version and launch a new session instead of attaching. Also, once a process
loads the gRPC client of one AEDT version it can never attach to another
version ([WinError 127] The specified procedure could not be found).

install() addresses this without modifying PyAEDT:

The default version becomes the newest installed AEDT, or the one chosen
with --aedt-version.

Attaching to a local port uses the version of the AEDT process on that port.

Attaching to a version the process can no longer load fails fast with an
actionable message.

title: The registry.py module > Description
text:
Description

File-backed registry of lane backends.

A lane is a long-lived ansys-aedt-mcp process serving the HTTP
transport on a loopback port. Each lane owns at most one AEDT session. The
registry records every running lane so that several MCP clients (IDE
windows, agents) can find and reuse the same backends.

The registry lives in a per-user state directory (%LOCALAPPDATA% on
Windows, $XDG_STATE_HOME on POSIX) and is guarded by a bounded-timeout
filelock.FileLock. A corrupt file is moved aside and replaced by an
empty registry, so every function here is safe to call from a recovery path.

Description

Detached HTML window for clients without MCP Apps support.

The HTML is written to a temporary wrapper file and opened in a chromeless
application window of an installed Microsoft Edge or Google Chrome browser.
If neither is found, the default browser is used.
Only the Python standard library is required.

The supplied HTML runs inside an iframe sandbox with an opaque origin and
a Content Security Policy that blocks network access, external resources,
forms, popups, and access to local files.

title: Best practices
text:
Best practices

Use these recommended patterns for PyAEDT-MCP to avoid common pitfalls,
improve performance, and build more robust workflows.

title: Best practices > Session management
text:
Session management

Reuse the AEDT connection.

Keep the same AEDT session open across multiple tool calls. Each
launch_aedt or connect_to_aedt call incurs a non-trivial startup
cost; only reconnect when genuinely necessary.

Check AEDT status before every workflow.

Always call check_aedt_status at the start of a workflow to confirm
whether an AEDT connection already exists. Use the result to decide
between launch_aedt (no session) and connect_to_aedt (existing
session).

Shut down cleanly.

Disconnect properly when done. Abrupt termination can leave AEDT processes
running and files in an inconsistent state. The active AEDT session stays
tied to the MCP server until you explicitly release it. If you do not
release it first, AEDT might not close normally from the UI. Use
disconnect_from_aedt for a graceful release or clear_aedt to also
close all open projects.

Check for errors.

Check the text returned by every tool for error messages before
proceeding. Most tools return a human-readable error string rather than
raising an exception, so the next step in a workflow can act on the result.

title: Best practices > Scripting with run_python_code
text:
Scripting with run_python_code

Use the persistent session.

run_python_script launches a separate CPython process with the connected
AEDT session’s environment. It does not share
Python variables with run_python_code. Check its returned output log
before starting dependent operations. Break complex workflows into short
run_python_code calls instead of one large script so you can inspect
intermediate state.

By default, PyAEDT-MCP applies settings.release_on_exception = False
in the execution session. This keeps the AEDT session alive when
generated code fails, which allows the AI agent to iterate and retry
fixes instead of losing the whole session.

Choose run_python_code over run_python_script.

Use run_python_code for short inline tasks. Reserve
run_python_script for files that already exist on disk (for example,
customer-provided scripts or parametric templates).

Use get_guidelines_for before you generate code.

When --include-context is active, call get_guidelines_for with the
relevant topic before writing PyAEDT code. The returned guidelines contain
correct API patterns, avoiding common mistakes.

AI-generated code can still close or destabilize a project unexpectedly in
some cases. Save your project frequently and keep a backup copy before
running larger generated code blocks.

title: Best practices > Data handling
text:
Data handling

Extract only what you need.

Query specific design properties or result values rather than loading
entire result sets. AEDT result files can be large; targeted extraction is
faster and less likely to hit tool timeouts.

Cache extracted data.

Store extracted data in Python variables within the persistent session so
subsequent analysis steps can reuse it without re-querying AEDT.

A recommended workflow is to extract the data you need, then disconnect
from AEDT when possible. This reduces risk, frees Desktop resources,
and lets you continue post-processing in Python without keeping AEDT
open longer than necessary.

title: Best practices > Visualization
text:
Visualization

Capture screenshots after key steps.

Call screenshot after geometry creation, after meshing, and after
analysis to give the AI assistant a visual checkpoint. This helps detect
geometry errors before solving.

Screenshots need the project to be saved beforehand. If the project is unsaved,
the screenshot tool returns an error.

Use run_python_code for custom plots.

For plots beyond what AEDT produces natively, use PyAEDT’s report API or
Matplotlib inside run_python_code. The persistent session keeps
previously imported libraries available.

Export artifacts for documentation.

Save high-quality screenshots and result plots with meaningful file names
so they can be included directly in engineering reports.

title: Best practices > Workflow design
text:
Workflow design

Break complex tasks into steps.

A well-structured workflow calls one dedicated tool per logical step
(connect → create design → set up geometry → analyze → export). This keeps
each tool call focused, makes errors easier to diagnose, and avoids timeout
issues.

Validate input before sending to AEDT.

Check parameter values (for example, frequencies, dimensions, materials)
in a run_python_code call before passing them to the solver. Early
validation avoids long solve runs that fail for trivial reasons.

Design for recovery.

Structure workflows so that individual steps can be re-run without
starting over. Use save_project after expensive geometry or mesh steps
to create recovery points.

title: Best practices > Performance
text:
Performance

Minimize AEDT restarts.

Relaunching AEDT adds tens of seconds of overhead. Reuse the existing
session across as many operations as possible.

Run independent analyses in parallel.

When running multiple independent designs (for example, a geometry sweep),
consider using AEDT’s built-in parametric solver rather than running
designs sequentially from the MCP server.

Process results in Python.

Extract result data into Python arrays or DataFrames and analyze it
there rather than issuing repeated AEDT queries. The persistent session
retains the data between calls.

async tools.find_api(queries: list[str], top_k: int = 5, scope: Literal['all', 'pyaedt', 'native'] = 'all', kinds: list[Literal['class', 'method', 'property', 'function']] | None = None, module: str | None = None, include_docstring: bool = False) -> str

Search the installed PyAEDT API offline, running up to 10 queries in parallel.

Use this tool before writing PyAEDT code to find the right class, method, or
property, and to map native AEDT scripting calls (oEditor.CreateBox,
oModule.AssignRadiation, oDesign.ExportNetworkData) to the PyAEDT
method that wraps them. Each hit includes the signature, a one-line summary,
the native AEDT calls the method uses, and the subclasses (such as Hfss)
that expose it. No AEDT connection is required.

Parameters

queries

python:list[python:str]

One to ten independent searches, run in parallel. Each query can be free
text ("radiation boundary"), a PyAEDT name ("create_box"), or a
native AEDT call ("oModule.InsertFrequencySweep").

top_k

python:int, default: 5

Maximum number of hits per query (1-25).

scope

python:str, default: "all"

"all" ranks by PyAEDT names, native calls, and docstrings.
"pyaedt" ignores native-call matching. "native" only returns
PyAEDT APIs that call a native AEDT API and favors native-name matches.

kinds

python:list[python:str], default: python:None

Restrict hits to class, method, property, or function.

module

python:str, default: python:None

Restrict hits to qualified names containing this text, for example
"ansys.aedt.core.hfss", "modeler", or "Hfss.".

include_docstring

bool, default: python:False

Whether to include the full docstring (parameters, returns, examples)
of each hit. Keep False for discovery and enable for the final pick.

text:
async tools.find_api(queries: list[str], top_k: int = 5, scope: Literal['all', 'pyaedt', 'native'] = 'all', kinds: list[Literal['class', 'method', 'property', 'function']] | None = None, module: str | None = None, include_docstring: bool = False) -> str

Search the installed PyAEDT API offline, running up to 10 queries in parallel.

Use this tool before writing PyAEDT code to find the right class, method, or
property, and to map native AEDT scripting calls (oEditor.CreateBox,
oModule.AssignRadiation, oDesign.ExportNetworkData) to the PyAEDT
method that wraps them. Each hit includes the signature, a one-line summary,
the native AEDT calls the method uses, and the subclasses (such as Hfss)
that expose it. No AEDT connection is required.

Parameters

queries

python:list[python:str]

One to ten independent searches, run in parallel. Each query can be free
text ("radiation boundary"), a PyAEDT name ("create_box"), or a
native AEDT call ("oModule.InsertFrequencySweep").

top_k

python:int, default: 5

Maximum number of hits per query (1-25).

scope

python:str, default: "all"

"all" ranks by PyAEDT names, native calls, and docstrings.
"pyaedt" ignores native-call matching. "native" only returns
PyAEDT APIs that call a native AEDT API and favors native-name matches.

kinds

python:list[python:str], default: python:None

Restrict hits to class, method, property, or function.

module

python:str, default: python:None

Restrict hits to qualified names containing this text, for example
"ansys.aedt.core.hfss", "modeler", or "Hfss.".

include_docstring

bool, default: python:False

Whether to include the full docstring (parameters, returns, examples)
of each hit. Keep False for discovery and enable for the final pick.

python:str

JSON string with one result block per query, in the same order as queries.

title: Lanes
text:
Lanes

By default, each MCP client starts its own PyAEDT-MCP server, which owns at
most one AEDT session. Lanes mode lets several MCP clients (for example
VS Code, Claude, and a terminal agent) share AEDT sessions, or run
isolated AEDT sessions side by side, from one machine.

Lanes mode is opt-in. It is enabled only by the --lanes argument. Without it,
PyAEDT-MCP behaves exactly as described in the rest of this guide.

title: Lanes > How it works
text:
How it works

A lane is a long-lived PyAEDT-MCP backend served over HTTP on
127.0.0.1. It owns at most one AEDT session.

ansys-aedt-mcp --lanes starts a small stdio routing proxy in each MCP
client. It exposes every regular PyAEDT-MCP tool plus lane management tools,
and forwards each AEDT tool call to the lane the client has selected.

Lanes are recorded in a per-user registry, so every client on the machine
sees the same lanes. Lanes survive client restarts.

No lane is spawned or selected at startup. The assistant calls
list_lanes and then switch_lane or spawn_lane before using AEDT.

title: Lanes > Security
text:
Security

Each lane is protected by a random bearer token, generated at spawn time and
stored in the per-user registry. Requests without the token are rejected
with HTTP 401.

The token is removed from the backend environment before AEDT starts, so
child processes never inherit it, and it is never returned by tools or the
status command.

Lanes bind to 127.0.0.1 by default.

title: Lanes > Configure your MCP client
text:
Configure your MCP client

Add --lanes to the arguments of the regular stdio configuration. For
example, in VS Code (.vscode/mcp.json):

Arguments after -- are forwarded to every lane backend, for example
["--lanes", "--", "--graphical", "--include-context"].

title: Lanes > Proxy options
text:
Proxy options

--http-host HOST

Host that lane backends bind to. The default is 127.0.0.1.

--startup-timeout SECONDS

Seconds a new lane gets to open its port. The default is 60.

--probe-timeout SECONDS

Seconds a lane gets to answer a status probe before it is reported as
unresponsive.

--handshake-timeout SECONDS

Seconds a lane gets to answer the MCP handshake. A busy lane is reported
as busy, and the call is not sent.

--aedt-version {latest,pyaedt,VERSION}

Default AEDT version used by lane backends: the newest installed version
(latest, the default), the PyAEDT default (pyaedt), or a version
such as 2026.1. Also read from ANSYS_AEDT_MCP_LANE_AEDT_VERSION.

--dynamic-tool-discovery cannot be forwarded to lanes. The proxy opens an
MCP session for each call, so AEDT-only tools would never be advertised.
--transport, --http-host, and --http-port are set by the proxy for
each lane and cannot be forwarded either.

title: Lanes > Lane management tools
text:
Lane management tools

These tools belong to the lanes toolset in toolsets://definition.





Tool

Purpose

list_lanes

List registered lanes with their health and AEDT session.

current_lane

Show the selected lane and any call in flight.

spawn_lane

Create a new lane and, by default, select it. It fails if the
name is already registered. It does not launch AEDT. Call launch_aedt
or connect_to_aedt next.

switch_lane

Select the lane that subsequent AEDT tool calls go to.

stop_lane

Shut down a lane backend.

check_lane

Diagnose a lane: listening, authentication, responsiveness, and AEDT state.

recycle_lane

Restart a lane backend and reattach it to the same AEDT session
without closing AEDT.

refresh_aedt_port

Re-read the AEDT gRPC port that a lane is attached to.

reap_lanes

Drop registry entries whose backend is no longer running.

reset_lanes

Clear the registry and optionally stop the lane processes.

unlock_registry_files

Delete a stale registry lock file.

filter-tuning), rather than default or a port number.

Recovery commands

The dashboard is a read-only local web page served on 127.0.0.1. It shows
whether each lane is up, busy, or degraded. It also shows the AEDT port and

State and logs

The registry, its lock file, and one lane-<port>.log per lane are stored in

title: The backend.py module > Description
text:
Description

Hooks that turn a regular HTTP server into a token-protected lane backend.

The lane spawner starts python -m ansys.aedt.mcp --transport http ...
with a per-lane secret in TOKEN_ENV. When server.launcher finds that variable, it calls
apply_lane_backend_hooks(). That function:

removes the secret from the environment so AEDT and any other child
process never inherit it,

requires the lane bearer token on every HTTP request, and

applies the PyAEDT version fixes from aedt_compat.

Without the variable, the server behaves exactly as before.

Tool

Description

check_aedt_installed

Check whether AEDT is installed on the system.

check_aedt_status

Report current connection state. Use before every workflow to decide
between launch_aedt and connect_to_aedt.

launch_aedt

Start a new AEDT instance. Pass application to create a design of
that type in the same call. The reply includes the open projects and

Maps native AEDT calls (such as oEditor.CreateBox) to PyAEDT methods.

Optional (enabled only with --lanes)

With ansys-aedt-mcp --lanes, all the preceding tools are routed to the

switch_lane, stop_lane, check_lane, recycle_lane, and others)

title: Tools and capabilities > Tool usage

title: Tools and capabilities > Display custom web content
text:
Display custom web content

Use display_html to render an HTML document or fragment. No AEDT
connection is required. For example:

Inline JavaScript and CSS are supported. The supplied HTML runs in a separate
sandbox: external resources, network requests, forms, popups, and access to the
MCP host are blocked. Embed images using data URLs. This tool does not run
Python or Matplotlib.

The display_mode argument controls where the HTML appears:

auto (default): inline when the client supports MCP Apps, otherwise in a
detached window.

inline: inline only. Clients without MCP Apps support receive a text
fallback and the HTML in structured content.

window: always open a detached window.

The inline viewer loads the MCP Apps SDK from https://unpkg.com, so that
domain must be reachable.

The detached window opens on the machine running the MCP server, using only the
Python standard library. It is an app window without browser controls, provided by
an installed Microsoft Edge or Google Chrome browser. If neither is found, the
default browser is used. To choose the browser, set the
PYAEDT_MCP_HTML_BROWSER environment variable to its executable. No window
is opened when the server runs in a container or without a graphical display.
The detached window resizes itself to fit the rendered HTML, limited to the
available screen area. Pass width (200-3840) or height (200-1200), in
pixels, to fix either dimension instead. Window resizing is not available when
falling back to the default browser. Views are written to the pyaedt-mcp-html-views temporary directory and
removed after 24 hours.

title: Tools and capabilities > Run inline PyAEDT code
text:
Run inline PyAEDT code

Use run_python_code for geometry creation, parameter updates, boundary
assignment, and any step that does not have a dedicated tool.

Your code runs in the persistent Python session of the current AEDT
instance. Imports and variables from one call are available in later calls.

Use run_python_script when you want to run a complete Python file in
a separate CPython process connected to the same AEDT session through the
PyAEDT launcher environment variables. It uses the MCP server’s Python
interpreter and opens no launcher UI or terminal. Native IronPython globals
such as oDesktop are not injected. The response contains the process ID
and an output log path, not a completion result; check the log before running
dependent operations. If a script is large, you can split it into smaller
chunks and run them with run_python_code.

title: Tools and capabilities > Search the PyAEDT API
text:
Search the PyAEDT API

Use find_api to locate PyAEDT classes, methods, and properties without
an AEDT connection. The tool indexes the installed PyAEDT package, so results
always match the version that runs your code. Each call accepts up to 10
queries, which run in parallel. A query can be free text, a PyAEDT name, or a
native AEDT scripting call. Each hit lists the signature, a summary, the native
AEDT calls that the method uses, and the subclasses (such as Hfss) that
expose it.

Set scope="native" to find the PyAEDT equivalent of native calls such as
oEditor.CreateBox or oModule.InsertFrequencySweep. Set
include_docstring=True to get the full parameter documentation of the hits.

“Search the PyAEDT API for length-based mesh operations and far-field exports.”

Every tool has a timeout guard so that a stalled AEDT call cannot hang the
server indefinitely.







Tier

open_project, save_project, create_design, validate_design,
screenshot, clear_aedt, and export_config

600 s

run_python_script, run_python_code, analyze_design,
and export_results

title: The api_search.py module > Description
text:
Description

Offline search over the PyAEDT API.

The index is built by statically parsing (ast) the installed
ansys.aedt.core package, so nothing is imported or executed. Each public
class, method, property, and function becomes one entry holding its signature,
docstring, and the native AEDT API calls it relies on. Native calls are
collected from two sources:

The References docstring section (for example >>> oModule.AssignRadiation).

Calls in the function body on AEDT COM objects (for example
self.oeditor.CreateBox(...)).

This makes it possible to search in both directions: from a PyAEDT concept to
the method that implements it, and from a native AEDT scripting call to the
PyAEDT method that wraps it.

Ranking uses BM25 over weighted name, native, summary, and docstring tokens,
plus boosts for exact name or native method matches.

title: Docker deployment
text:
Docker deployment

You can run PyAEDT-MCP as a containerized service with HTTP transport.
Because AEDT does not have a publicly available Docker image, the MCP
container connects to an AEDT instance running on your host machine or on a
remote server.

The HTTP transport has no authentication or encryption. Any client that can
reach the port can call every tool with no credential, including
run_python_code (arbitrary Python execution against the connected AEDT
session) and tools that read or write attacker-chosen local paths, such as
open_project, save_project, and export_results. Never publish this
port on a network you do not fully trust, or on the public internet. Only
expose it beyond localhost if it is placed behind a reverse proxy (such as
Nginx or HAProxy) that provides both TLS/SSL and its own authentication
(for example mutual TLS or an authenticating gateway). The Docker Compose file
included in this repository publishes the port on 127.0.0.1 only, so it is
not reachable from other machines by default.

helpers.install_fast_process_lookup() -> bool

Make PyAEDT’s Windows AEDT process lookup use psutil instead of tasklist.

PyAEDT resolves AEDT PIDs on Windows by spawning tasklist (about 2 s per call).
That lookup runs in loops while launching AEDT (is_grpc_session_active once per
second), while closing it (while pid in active_sessions()), and when attaching to
a session. Replacing it with an equivalent psutil scan (a few milliseconds)
removes seconds of dead time from launch_aedt, connect_to_aedt, and
disconnect_from_aedt. The patch is a no-op outside Windows or if PyAEDT
internals change.

Add a new tool

This example shows how to add a new @app.tool(...) safely and make it visible
at the right stages of an MCP session.

title: Add a new tool > Where to implement
text:
Where to implement

Add the tool implementation to src/ansys/aedt/mcp/tools.py.

Add the tool to the appropriate group in src/ansys/aedt/mcp/toolsets.py.

Document the tool behavior in ../user_guide/tools_and_capabilities.

title: Add a new tool > Decorator options and tags
text:
Decorator options and tags

Use FastMCP’s @app.tool(...) decorator with these key options:

tags: Set of tags used for grouping and runtime filtering.

timeout: Maximum execution time for the tool.

Use these common tags in this repository:

REQUIRES_AEDT_TAG: Mark tools that require an active AEDT connection.

aedt_tools: Group core AEDT-facing tools.

locked_connection: Mark tools that are disabled when startup uses
--connect and locks the connection for the server lifetime.

Use these timeout tiers in this repository:

Quick: 30 seconds

Medium: 120 seconds

Long: 600 seconds

title: Add a new tool > Runtime flags and their effect
text:
Runtime flags and their effect

Server startup flags affect tool visibility and behavior:

--dynamic-tool-discovery: Hide REQUIRES_AEDT_TAG tools until AEDT
connects.

--connect: Connect at startup and lock the session. In this mode,
launch_aedt, connect_to_aedt, and disconnect_from_aedt are
disabled for the life of the process.

--include-context: Register optional context tools such as
get_guidelines_for.
